items.title: Importing and exporting
items.source: Draft for review. Written by an AI assistant from general UK small-business knowledge, not from a cited document. Check every fact against current GOV.UK and regulator guidance, and have someone who does this work review it, before it is activated. Rules differ by country and change.
items.body: Moving goods across borders adds steps and costs. Each shipment needs a customs declaration and a commodity code that classifies the goods, which decides the duty rate and any restrictions. You may owe import duty and VAT on arrival, and need a registration number to import or export (in the UK, an EORI number). Incoterms are standard shipping terms that say who pays for transport, insurance and customs at each point, and where risk passes from seller to buyer. Include duty, freight, insurance and fees in your price, or your margin disappears. A freight forwarder or customs broker can handle the paperwork.

options.text: Classifies goods, which decides duty and any restrictions

Standard shipping terms saying who pays for what and when risk passes

questions.prompt: Why include duty and freight in your selling price?

options.text: Otherwise the margin on the sale disappears
They are always paid by the customer's bank

questions.prompt: Who can help with customs paperwork?

options.text: A freight forwarder or customs broker

items.title: Fulfilling your first orders
items.source: Draft for review. Written by an AI assistant from general UK small-business knowledge, not from a cited document. Check every fact against current GOV.UK and regulator guidance, and have someone who does this work review it, before it is activated. Rules differ by country and change.
items.body: Your first orders are a test of the whole process, so treat them that way. Before the first order, write down each step from enquiry to delivery and invoice: confirm the order, check stock, make or prepare, pack, send, tell the customer, invoice and collect payment. Confirm price, delivery date and what is included in writing. Keep a simple record of each order and of anything that went wrong. After delivery, ask the customer how it went and note what you would change. Fix the process before the tenth order, not after the hundredth. Heroics that work once do not scale.

items.title: Scaling operations
items.source: Draft for review. Written by an AI assistant from general UK small-business knowledge, not from a cited document. Check every fact against current GOV.UK and regulator guidance, and have someone who does this work review it, before it is activated. Rules differ by country and change.
items.body: Scaling means handling more customers without a drop in quality or an equal rise in cost. First find the bottleneck, the step that limits output, and fix it first; improving anything else does not help. Write down and simplify processes so new people can follow them. Automate repeated, low-skill work and keep people for judgement and care. Train and supervise before you add volume. Watch quality and customer satisfaction as numbers grow, and add capacity ahead of demand but not too far ahead. Scale in steps and check after each, because what worked at ten customers often breaks at a hundred.

questions.prompt: What does scaling mean?

options.text: Handling more customers without losing quality or raising costs at the same rate

questions.prompt: What is a bottleneck?

options.text: The step that limits how much you can produce

questions.prompt: Why write down and simplify processes before scaling?

options.text: It removes the need for training
New people can follow them and quality holds

options.text: What works at ten customers often breaks at a hundred
Steps are cheaper in every case

items.body: Closing premises is one of the last jobs when a business winds down, and it has deadlines. Check your lease for notice periods, break clauses and any duty to restore the property, and tell the landlord in writing. Plan stock: sell it, return it to suppliers where allowed, donate or dispose of it properly, and keep records. Deal with equipment you own or lease, and clear all personal data from devices before they leave. Cancel utilities, insurance and services in the right order and take final meter readings. Photograph the empty premises and hand back keys with a signed record.

items.title: Choosing premises and equipment
items.source: Draft for review. Written by an AI assistant from general UK small-business knowledge, not from a cited document. Check every fact against current GOV.UK and regulator guidance, and have someone who does this work review it, before it is activated. Rules differ by country and change.
items.body: Before committing to premises and equipment, work out what you really need and what it will cost over time. For premises, compare location, size, rent, rates, lease length, break options, repair duties and any rules on use. Never sign a lease without reading it carefully and, where possible, having it checked. For equipment, compare buying, leasing and second-hand, and count maintenance, insurance and the cost if it breaks. Check safety and legal requirements for the way you will use them. Start with what you need now and avoid long commitments for the business you hope to have.

options.text: Your needs may differ, and a long commitment is hard to leave

items.title: The weekly review
items.source: Draft for review. Written by an AI assistant from general UK small-business knowledge, not from a cited document. Check every fact against current GOV.UK and regulator guidance, and have someone who does this work review it, before it is activated. Rules differ by country and change.
items.body: A weekly review is a short routine, often thirty minutes, that keeps the business under control. Look at last week's results: sales, cash, orders delivered, problems. Check the plan for the coming week and name the three most important things. Review open items and decide to do, hand on or drop each. Look at your cash position and any bills or payments due. Note anything customers said. Write down the actions, each with a name and a date, and keep the notes brief. Do it at the same time each week, even when busy; that is when it matters most.
